title: How to Start Investing If You’re a U.S. Freelancer or Gig Worker
description: Navigating the Solo 401(k), SEP IRA, and lack of employer matching.
content:
For traditional employees, investing is easy: sign up for the 401(k), get the match, and forget it. For the 60 million US freelancers, gig workers, and contractors, it is much harder. You have no HR department, no automatic deductions, and no free money match. However, you have a secret weapon: The US Tax Code. The government offers self-employed individuals massive tax-advantaged accounts that actually allow you to save *more* than a W-2 employee—if you know which forms to file.

Key Takeaways

  • The Solo 401(k) is King: It allows you to contribute as both the 'Employee' ($23k) AND the 'Employer' (20% of profits), totaling up to $69,000 (2025 limit).
  • SEP IRA is Simpler: Easier paperwork than a Solo 401(k) but lacks the 'Catch-Up' contribution feature and Roth option usually.
  • Automate the 'Tax & Save': Since you don't have payroll, you must manually transfer a % of every invoice to investments immediately.
  • The 'Buffer' is Critical: Freelancers need a larger cash cushion (6-9 months) before investing aggressively due to income volatility.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Self-employed Americans pay the 15.3% Self-Employment Tax (Social Security/Medicare). Contributions to a Traditional Solo 401(k) or SEP IRA reduce your taxable income, effectively giving you a massive discount on your tax bill. A $10,000 contribution might save you $3,000 in taxes instantly.

Solo 401(k) vs. SEP IRA vs. SIMPLE IRA

Choosing the right vehicle is the first step.

1. Solo 401(k) (Best for High Savings)

  • Limit: Up to $69,000.
  • Pros: Roth option available. Loans allowed (borrow from yourself).
  • Cons: More paperwork. Must have EIN. Must file Form 5500 if assets > $250k.
  • Best For: Solopreneurs with no employees (except spouse).

2. SEP IRA (Best for Simplicity)

  • Limit: 25% of net profit (up to $69k).
  • Pros: easy setup at Fidelity/Vanguard. No annual filing.
  • Cons: No Roth option (usually). If you hire employees later, you MUST contribute to their SEP too (expensive).

3. Traditional / Roth IRA

  • Limit: $7,000.
  • Pros: Anyone with income can use it.
  • Cons: Low limit. Not enough for full retirement. Use this in addition to the above.

The 'Income Waterfall' for Freelancers

  1. Step 1: Open Business Checking. Never mix personal and business money.
  2. Step 2: The 30% Tax Hold. Every time an invoice hits, move 30% to a 'Tax Savings' account. Do not touch it.
  3. Step 3: The Paycheck. Transfer a fixed salary to your personal checking.
  4. Step 4: The Profit Sweep. At the end of the quarter, take the remaining profit. Put 50% into your Solo 401(k) and 50% into a Business Emergency Fund.
  5. Step 5: File Quarterly. Use the cash in Step 2 to pay estimated taxes. If you over-saved, invest the difference.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I have a Solo 401(k) if I also have a W-2 job?

Yes! But the 'Employee' contribution limit ($23k) is shared across all 401(k)s. If you max out at your day job, your side hustle Solo 401(k) can only receive 'Employer' profit-sharing contributions.

Do I need an LLC to open these?

Usually no. A Sole Proprietorship with an EIN (Employer Identification Number) is sufficient. You can get an EIN from the IRS website in 5 minutes for free.

What if I hire a contractor?

Contractors (1099) do not count as employees, so they don't disqualify you from a Solo 401(k). Only W-2 employees disqualify you.
